name: The Mill
description:
Muskegon was a lumber town, then a manufacturing town, then a town that wasn't sure what it was. By 2200 it has finally figured it out: Muskegon is a machine. Specifically, it is a machine for moving things from the lake to the land and from the land to the lake, and for processing whatever passes through its gears in between.

The port -- now operated by Axiom Industries' Great Lakes Logistics Division -- handles 30% of all eastern Lake Michigan cargo traffic. The old lumber mill sites along Muskegon Lake have been converted into automated processing facilities: raw materials arrive by cargo ship, are sorted by AI-managed systems, loaded onto maglev freight cars, and distributed inland along the corridor before a human hand touches any of it. The efficiency is remarkable. The employment figures are not. Axiom's port operations employ roughly 800 people in a city of 60,000, and most of those positions are supervisory roles monitoring systems that could monitor themselves.

What Muskegon has that automation can't replace is geography. The Muskegon Lake channel is the deepest harbor on the eastern shore, capable of receiving cargo vessels that can't dock anywhere between here and the Straits. This makes the Mill a chokepoint -- and chokepoints breed economies. The harbor district is a dense, rough, functional zone of bars, equipment suppliers, repair docks, and the kind of services that people who spend weeks on automated cargo ships need when they finally hit land. It's not pretty. It doesn't try to be. Muskegon has the honest ugliness of a place that does real work, and there is a certain respect in the lakefront communities for a town that never pretended to be anything other than what it is.

The residential districts south of the port have the character of a city that has been through so many economic cycles that it has stopped flinching at the next one. The houses are old, maintained with stubbornness rather than money. The community organizations predate every corporate era and will outlast the current one. Muskegon endures. It does not thrive. It endures, and that is its own form of strength.

sights: Cargo cranes along the Muskegon Lake channel, moving containers in patterns that look choreographed because they are -- AI-optimized, inhuman in their efficiency
The harbor district at night -- neon and sodium light reflecting off wet pavement, the only part of town that's genuinely alive after dark
Automated processing facilities on the old lumber mill sites, windowless and massive, humming with activity that requires no human witness
Muskegon Lake itself, an industrial waterway connecting the port to Lake Michigan, its surface frequently sheened with cargo runoff
The residential south side -- 20th-century housing stock stubbornly maintained, American flags and union flags on the same porches
sounds: Cargo operations -- clanking, grinding, the bass note of massive ships settling into berths
The harbor district's bars, spilling noise into the street -- the universal soundtrack of port towns
Automated systems communicating in data bursts that sound like mechanical birdsong
Wind off Lake Michigan channeled through the Muskegon Lake corridor, amplified and salt-heavy
Church bells on Sunday, still rung in a town that maintains its traditions the way it maintains its houses -- through effort, not funding
smells: Industrial harbor -- diesel, rust, lubricant, the honest smell of machinery
Lake Michigan through the channel, carrying whatever the automated cargo ships are leaking today
The harbor district's food -- fried everything, smoked fish, coffee that could strip paint
Sawdust, impossibly -- a ghost smell from the lumber mill era that residents swear is real
atmosphere.feel: Working-class and unashamed of it. The Mill doesn't have the desperate edge of the Slagshore or the manufactured pleasantness of Ironhaven. It has the specific gravity of a place where people know what they are and don't waste energy pretending otherwise. There's a toughness here that isn't aggressive -- it's structural, built into the community the way the lake is built into the geography. You come to the Mill to work. You stay because it doesn't lie to you.

demographics: Approximately 60,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1-2. Historically diverse working-class population with strong multi-generational community ties. Axiom port personnel are Tier 3, housed in a separate compound near the facilities. Significant veteran population from the Corporate Consolidation conflicts.
economy: Axiom port operations dominate -- Φ4.2 billion in annual cargo throughput. Local economy survives on harbor services, ship repair, and a gray market in cargo 'samples' that fall off manifests during processing. The gap between the port's revenue and the city's poverty is Muskegon's defining economic feature.
power_structure: Axiom Industries holds sovereign authority over the port facilities and Muskegon Lake channel. The city retains nominal municipal governance over residential districts. The actual power broker is the Harbor Workers' Association, a hybrid of union, mutual aid society, and organized crime that controls access to the gray market cargo economy and provides social services the city government cannot afford.
dangers: The harbor district after dark -- functional but rough, with the predictable hazards of any port town's entertainment zone
Axiom automated security in the port zone -- efficient, impersonal, and programmed to prioritize cargo protection over human safety
The Harbor Workers' Association demands respect and reciprocity -- cross them and the port becomes very unfriendly
Industrial contamination from the processing facilities -- respiratory issues are endemic
Lake storms hitting the Muskegon channel -- the geography that makes the port valuable also makes it a funnel for extreme weather
opportunities: The gray cargo market moves significant volume and value for those with the right Harbor Workers' Association connections
Ship repair skills are in high demand and command premium rates
The Mill's geographic chokepoint means information about lake traffic flows through here -- valuable intelligence for anyone interested in what's moving on the water
Axiom's automated systems have patterns and gaps that experienced operators have mapped over decades
story_hooks: An automated cargo ship docks with a manifest that doesn't match its contents -- and the contents are alive
The Harbor Workers' Association is being quietly bought out by a corponation that wants to control the gray market rather than eliminate it
A storm damages one of the old lumber mill foundations, revealing a sealed sublevel that predates the digital era and contains records that someone walled up deliberately

adjacent_to: Ironhaven / Grand Haven (south along the coast)
Ludington / The Crossing (north along the coast)
Inland corridor communities (east, via maglev freight line)

frequented_by: Cargo ship crews on shore leave
Harbor Workers' Association members running the gray market
Axiom logistics supervisors monitoring automated systems
Freelance operators looking for cargo work or information
